opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and I really appreciate the work Charles and Michael have done. Their heavy-tailed self-regularization line of research, the WeightWatcher tool, is really a beautiful example of how much information is sitting in the weights themselves. They look at the empirical spectral density of the weight matrices, the eigenvalue distributions of each layer, and they fit power laws to them. From the shape of those distributions they can say something about how well a layer is trained, whether it's over- or under-regularized, and even predict generalization quality without touching any test data. So it's very principled, grounded in random matrix theory and statistical mechanics.

Where we differ is mostly in the philosophy of how you extract that information. Their approach is analytical. You hand-design the metric, say the power-law exponent alpha, and you compute it layer by layer. What we do is treat the weights as a data modality in their own right. We collected what we call model zoos, large populations of trained networks, thousands of models trained with different seeds, hyperparameters, and so on, and saved checkpoints along their training trajectories. Then we train neural networks on those weights. We use things like hyper-representations, essentially autoencoders or transformer-based encoders that take tokenized weights as input and learn an embedding space of models.

So instead of saying, here's the one statistic we think matters, we let a model learn what's relevant from the population. And once you have that learned representation, you can do more than diagnose. You can predict accuracy or generalization gap, infer hyperparameters, or detect which training stage a model is in. And because it's generative, you can sample new weights from that space and use them to initialize models, sometimes faster or better than random initialization.

There's also a structural point. Spectral analysis is nicely invariant to some of the symmetries in neural networks, like permutations of neurons, because eigenvalues don't care about ordering. In our learned setting we have to deal with those symmetries explicitly. Permutation symmetry, scaling symmetries, all of that. So we've put a lot of effort into augmentations and architectures that respect them, kind of like you'd do data augmentation in computer vision.

So I'd see the two as complementary. Their work gives you theory-driven, interpretable diagnostics that work on a single model. Ours is more data-driven, needs populations of models, but in return gives you a richer, task-flexible representation, and the ability to generate weights, not just analyze them. And honestly, I think there's a nice opportunity to combine them, for instance using spectral features as inputs or as inductive biases for weight-space models.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Martin and Mahoney’s hand-designed spectral metrics with Borth’s approach of training neural networks to learn representations from populations of model weights.

r002.rationale: It mentions model zoos and varied trained networks, but does not propose training a foundation model from heterogeneous models in open-weight repositories such as Hugging Face.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and I actually get it a lot, because on the surface it looks like we're doing the same thing — we're all staring at weights instead of staring at data. But I think the goals, and then as a consequence the methods, are quite different.

So what Charles and Michael did, which I really admire, is essentially a theory-driven analysis. They take the weight matrices of a trained network, layer by layer, compute the empirical spectral density — the eigenvalue distribution of the correlation matrix — and then fit that against heavy-tailed random matrix theory. And from that they derive these metrics, the alpha exponent and so on, that tell you something about how well-trained a layer is, whether it's over- or under-fit, and they can do that without ever looking at test data. It's a very elegant, hand-designed diagnostic. You know in advance what statistic you're computing, and the statistic is grounded in a theory about what training does to the weights.

What we do is, I would say, much more in the spirit of representation learning. We don't start with a hypothesis about which property of the weights matters. We treat the weights themselves as a data modality. So we collect what we call model zoos — hundreds or thousands of networks, same architecture, trained with different seeds, different hyperparameters, different datasets — and then we train a second model, an encoder, on top of those weights. Self-supervised, mostly, so contrastive objectives, reconstruction, permutation augmentations because of all the symmetries in weight space. And the question we ask is: can that model discover, on its own, a representation of the weights that carries information about the original network? Its accuracy, its generalization gap, what data it was trained on, even what kind of adversarial robustness it has.

So one way I like to put it is: they're doing feature engineering on weights, and they're doing it extremely well. We're trying to learn the features. And those are complementary. In fact, their spectral metrics are a very natural baseline for us, and in several of our experiments they're among the strongest handcrafted baselines. Sometimes we beat them, sometimes they're very close, and honestly when a learned representation and a theory-grounded statistic agree, that's a good sign for both.

The other difference is what you do downstream. Their work is mainly about analysis and prediction — assessing a model. For us the learned embedding space opens up a second direction, which is generation. Once you have a latent space over weights, you can sample from it, you can interpolate, you can decode back into weights and get a new network that actually works, or use it as an initialization that trains faster. That's not something a spectral statistic gives you, because it's a summary — you can't invert it back into a model. So I'd say their line of work is closer to a diagnostic instrument, and we're trying to build something more like a generative, learned understanding of the population of models — but I'd be the first to say we stand on top of what they showed, which is that the weights really do contain this information in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Martin and Mahoney’s theory-driven, hand-designed spectral analysis with Borth’s learned encoder that discovers representations of weights.

r002.rationale: It describes training an encoder on model zoos with varied seeds, hyperparameters, and datasets, but does not raise training a foundation model from heterogeneous models in open-weight repositories such as Hugging Face.

astra-6.text: The connection is that we both look at the weights of a neural network rather than just its outputs. But I would distinguish analyzing weights from learning on weights. Martin and Mahoney’s work uses spectral analysis to study the structure of weight matrices and what that structure can tell us about a network. In our approach, the weights themselves become the data for another learning problem. We take a population of trained networks and learn a representation of those networks in weight space. So there’s a shared starting point, but a different emphasis: understanding the structure of an individual network versus learning across networks.

r001.rationale: It contrasts Martin and Mahoney’s spectral analysis of weight matrices with Borth’s approach of learning representations across a population of trained networks.

r002.rationale: It does not raise training a foundation model from heterogeneous open-weight models or mention repositories such as Hugging Face.

sol-6.1.text:
The main distinction is that Charles Martin and Michael Mahoney analyze the weights to understand the properties of a neural network. They look at the spectral structure of weight matrices and use that to say something about training and generalization.

What we’re doing is treating the weights themselves as data for another learning problem. Instead of designing an analysis of a particular weight matrix, we learn a representation across a population of trained neural networks. We call those representations hyper-representations. The idea is that they capture information about the networks that we can then use for downstream tasks, such as predicting their properties.

So there’s a shared starting point—the information contained in the weights—but a different emphasis: analyzing that structure versus learning a representation of it.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts Martin and Mahoney analyzing weight structure with Borth learning representations from weights across trained networks.

r002.rationale: It does not raise the possibility of training a foundation model from heterogeneous neural networks in open-weight repositories such as Hugging Face.
